title: Anthropic Economic Index 2026—Measuring Claude Usage with “Economic Primitives” Metrics
summary: Summary of Anthropic's 2026 Economic Index: usage concentrated in coding, larger speedups but lower success on complex tasks, net deskilling, and a modest productivity estimate.

assertions.quote: A whopping 34% of all tasks are in computer and mathematical fields. We're talking coding, software development, that kind of thing.

verdicts.note: Anthropic's own usage data and other usage studies consistently find coding is the largest single category.

assertions.quote: AI is spreading like wildfire, about 10 times faster than major technologies from the last century.

verdicts.note: Survey data show unusually fast uptake of generative AI, though comparisons with past technologies depend on how adoption is defined.

assertions.quote: The data shows that AI gives the biggest speed boosts on the hard stuff, the more complex, higher-skill work.

verdicts.note: Consistent across Stanford's data, METR's mature-repo slowdown and long-context degradation results.

assertions.quote: The success rate actually drops. It goes from 70% on simpler stuff down to 66% on the hard stuff.

verdicts.note: Benchmarks, METR task-horizon work and usage studies all show success falling with task length and complexity.

METR 2025, qualitative: developers say AI does worse in complex settings, e.g. a refactor that was 'too big' where AI 'introduced as many errors as it fixed', and failures tied to file size. These are anecdotes, not success rates.
Airbnb: simple files passed with a few retries, complex ones needed rich context, and the last ~100 files hit a ceiling after 50-100 retries and were fixed by hand.
GPT-4 alone solved all five easy experiment tasks but got two of five harder APPS interview/competition tasks wrong, and the AI-assisted accuracy gain shrank on the harder set (tiny task sample).

assertions.quote: Right now, the net effect across the entire economy is actually deskilling.

verdicts.note: This is a model-based estimate from one vendor's usage data; independent labor-market evidence on deskilling versus upskilling is not yet clear.

assertions.quote: once you adjust for how often AI actually succeeds in the real world, the number comes down to a more realistic 1%.

verdicts.note: This is a projection built on model-estimated task speedups; macro productivity data has not yet confirmed effects of this size.

assertions.quote: Just giving everyone access to AI isn't going to cut it. That's not enough.

verdicts.note: Adoption and gains vary widely across teams and DORA finds organizational practices matter, but evidence isolating training effects is mostly observational.

With access alone only 8.5% of Microsoft's treated developers signed up in two weeks; reminder emails lifted it to 42.5%, Accenture's training plus manager encouragement sped adoption, and 30-40% never tried the tool despite free access.

Developers varied in how effectively they used AI (habitual users got the CodeHealth benefit), which authors take to mean training developers in these tools remains important; this is about individual skill, not organizational rollout.
Google notes that bespoke AI use has a hidden cost of training engineers in the techniques and that tooling to hide AI is costly to maintain, which only touches on enablement.
